<reason>Both sides were sharp, but PRO kept the debate anchored to the motion as written: a counterfactual comparison of the same city with versus without two decades of legal supply, under a "more affordable, not perfectly affordable" standard. CON's strongest move—demanding a real-world metro that legalized infill twenty years ago and is cheaper today—was answered squarely: no such experiment was ever run, so the evidence must be comparative. CON's Seattle/Denver/Austin evidence (built a lot, still got expensive) never engaged the counterfactual; PRO's "that measures demand growth, not supply's effect" landed, and CON's closing reply ("exactly, demand swamps every unit") effectively committed CON to the extreme claim that supply cannot discipline prices in superstar metros, which PRO's Q2 and closing line ("the only good whose price ignores its quantity") exposed. CON had genuinely good material—option-value capitalization, the sprawl-vs-density distinction on Houston/Phoenix, bubble amplification, PRO's inconsistency on the price-to-income metric—but CON asserted these forces without weighing them to show the net effect exceeds two decades of compounding stock. PRO's "busts are cyclical, bans are permanent" asymmetry did that weighing. CON's clipped Rebuttal 1 was a small additional execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1/A2 in Rebuttal 2 and closing: answering "name an instance" by noting the ban itself prevented the experiment, then reframing Seattle-with-cranes vs Seattle-without as the only comparison the motion asks, with "the 2009 vacancy is gone; the 2009 building still shelters someone tonight" neutralizing CON's crash argument.</best_rebuttal>
